report:
## Conclusion: supported by strong evidence

Yes. The adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV; Shingrix) substantially reduces shingles (herpes zoster) in adults aged **70 years or older**.

The pivotal evidence is the international, phase 3 **ZOE-70** randomized, observer-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Participants received two doses of vaccine or placebo. The trial found that vaccination reduced both shingles and postherpetic neuralgia (a persistent pain complication) in this age group. The FDA’s prescribing information reports that efficacy in people ≥70 was assessed using a prespecified pooled analysis of the two pivotal trials; published trial results reported approximately **91% efficacy** against shingles in this group.

This is particularly meaningful because shingles risk and complications increase with age, while the previous live zoster vaccine had much lower effectiveness in older adults. CDC recommends two RZV doses for immunocompetent adults aged 50 and older.

Important qualifications: the efficacy figure is from controlled trials in people who completed the two-dose series, so it is not a guarantee for every individual. Local and systemic short-term reactions are common, and post-licensure CDC surveillance confirms these reactions; safety decisions should account for personal contraindications and prior severe allergic reactions.

Follow-up of the ZOE-50/ZOE-70 cohorts indicates protection remains high for years, including an interim analysis approximately 10 years after vaccination—supporting that the benefit is not merely short-lived.
